issues.issue: "immediate family shall include" is an inclusive rather than exhaustive formula, so whether relatives outside the long list qualify is open. The proviso that the three days "fall within the regularly scheduled work-week" also leaves partial entitlement unaddressed.

Foremen and assistant foremen are placed on seniority and priority lists here, yet Section 6-B makes the terms of their employment a matter of individual agreement and gives the Publisher an unrestricted right of removal. The two treat supervisory status inconsistently.

"Otherwise seniority is herein defined as length of service based on regularity and continuity of service" gives a second and different meaning of seniority from 4-A.1(a)'s length of service in a regular situation. The word "Otherwise" does not say when each definition applies.

Section 4-B fills vacant regular situations "in accord with their seniority standing," while this paragraph assigns claims to newly created or vacant situations to promotional priority, not seniority. The two allocation rules point to different men.

Group 1 admits men who lost a situation "because of illness, physical incapacity or for other such good and sufficient cause" — a general catch-all after two specifics whose reach is left to the Adjustment Board. Group 3's "men who signify their intention to and do shape steadily" is equally unquantified.

The promotion order lists only Group 1 and Group 3, omitting Groups 2 and 4 that appear in the hiring order, inviting an expressio unius argument that they can never be promoted. Nothing states whether the omission is deliberate.

Section 4-B says vacant situations are filled permanently from among regular situation holders by qualification and seniority, while this subsection is the source of promotion from the extra groups. The interaction of the two routes to a situation is unresolved.
"except where competency is a factor" carves an undefined exception out of the failure-to-shape rule that governs delisting. Whether a man was passed over for competence is not made determinable.

The paragraph makes the Adjustment Board the only body that may add to or change the lists, then allows a foreman to "engage such men as he may be able to obtain" off-list when short-handed. The exclusivity and the foreman's free hand are hard to read together.

The definition of "industry" is syntactically broken — "all companies employing persons engaged in the categories contained in Section 2 hereof by any Publisher, newspaper distributor or wholesaler" — so it is unclear whether the qualifier limits the companies or the persons. A defined term used throughout Section 4 turns on that reading.

The two allocations — one third for non-signatory transfers and two thirds for signatory transfers — are printed as "(4)" and "(34)", so the fractions as written do not correspond to the words. The arithmetic of the annual cap depends on which is right.
"qualified and competent for the work or the job in question" is nowhere defined, and the Agreement provides only that disputes about it go to the Board. The standard itself carries no content.

"the subsequent vacancies not in excess of five created by filling it" and the direction that "the last such subsequent vacancy shall be filled only by a relayman, relief man, bulldog routeman or floorman" leave the sequence of moves genuinely uncertain. The paragraph also says the job is filled "immediately" and then only at the end of a four-week posting.

This section fills vacancies permanently "in accord with their seniority standing," whereas 4-A.1(b) says promotional priority, not seniority, determines who may claim a newly created or vacant regular situation. The two rules select different claimants.

"partial incapacitation by reason of advanced age" and "a leave of absence from the industry" are undefined excusing conditions on which loss of a situation turns. Whether a given absence falls inside them cannot be read off the text.

This paragraph deems the situation vacated automatically after ninety or one hundred twenty days, while subsection (c) makes vacancy depend on a certified letter and a thirty-day explanation period. The "subject to Subsection (c)" tag does not say which date controls.
"shall not be unreasonably withheld" governs both consent and extension without any stated criteria. What refusal is reasonable is left wholly at large.
The situation is preserved "unless an explanation for the absence is received," with no requirement that the explanation be adequate or accepted. Any response would literally defeat the vacancy.

"Employees absent for the foregoing reasons" does not say whether it means only the four excused reasons in 4-F.1(a) or any absence described in that paragraph. Restoration rights turn on that reading.
The weekly maximum is printed as "8915 hours," which is not a possible figure and must stand for thirty-nine and one-half. The written cap on the day work week is therefore not stated in usable form.

"so that as many regular situations as possible may be created and maintained" imposes a duty with no measurable limit — "as possible" is judged against nothing. Whether a given schedule complies is pure argument.

Section 3-D.1 recognises the Publisher's right at any time to reduce routes and lay off for economic reasons, while 3-D.6 expressly preserves the maintenance obligation created here. The right to cut and the duty to maintain govern the same conduct.

This paragraph pays double time for advance-section work on Sunday between 10:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m., while 5-K pays time and one-half for Sunday work in exactly the same hours. The two rates cover overlapping work with no priority stated.

Section 16-M.3 forbids any change in condition without the other party's prior consent, whereas this section lets the Publisher change starting times and days off on four days' notice (or pay a premium). Whether a starting-time change needs Union consent is left open.

Section 5-I requires double the regular and overtime rates for advance-section work in the identical Sunday 10:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. window that this section pays at time and one-half. The instrument does not say which rate applies to that work.

"sufficiently far from where it began to involve substantial travel time" states a threshold with no measure, and the compensation is left to be negotiated later. The provision creates an obligation whose content does not yet exist.

"required or distributed unfairly" is the only limit on the employer's power to compel overtime and carries no stated content. The clause both mandates overtime and makes its imposition challengeable on an undefined ground.

"Present practice regarding the paid lunch period shall prevail as to an outside employee" leaves the entitlement of outside employees wholly undefined and undated. Inside employees get a precise rule and outside employees none.

Foremen's hours and wages are made a matter of private agreement here, yet 4-A.1(a) places foremen on the seniority and priority lists and Section 13 fixes wage scales for the Section 2 operations they may perform. The two schemes overlap without a stated priority.

Only the foreman or assistant-in-charge may "make changes in operating procedures," while 16-M.3 forbids any change in condition without the other party's consent. Whether a foreman's procedural change is a prohibited change in condition is not addressed.

"or days observed as such" is undefined, leaving open when a holiday is treated as falling on another day. The inline definition of an employee who "trips" also turns on the undefined phrase "obtains employment elsewhere in the industry."

The holiday runs from the start of the night shift the night before to the end of the day shift of the holiday, but 5-B defines the night shift as running from 6:00 p.m. to 10:00 a.m., so part of the holiday-night shift falls on the holiday itself. The boundaries of the two definitions do not align.

The premium is written as "price and one-half of the holiday rate," which is not a rate at all and must be read as time and one-half. The sentence as written does not state what the employee is paid after the regular shift.

The bar on rearranging work weeks in a holiday week cannot be squared with 5-J, which lets the Publisher change days off on four days' notice. The exclusion for sick leave also cites "Section 18-B.2," a section that does not exist (sick leave is defined in 13-B.2).

Section 7-C guarantees any employee required to work a holiday "not less than two (2) days' pay for the regular shift worked," while this section pays double the regular and overtime rates when the paper is not issued. Whether the two stack or are the same entitlement is unstated.
